title: The Grand Expedition: the Talk, the decision and the handover
summary: Ten minutes and four acts, opening cold with a voice from the start of the arc; then the family debates a motion they wrote and they judge it alone and read the decision aloud; then the Autumn Protocol goes over in their own handwriting, the Atlas closes on the capsule, and they produce and run the Sprout's showcase.
materials: the Expedition dossier, open at the run of show
four props, one per act: the season 1 badge, the season 2 adder, the season 3 closed ledger, and one thing from this season that you pick
the cold open, prepared and settled before today, and not opened again since
the sealed envelope with your motions inside it, and a blank ballot
the Autumn Protocol, written out on one page in your own handwriting
the Field Atlas, the time capsule and the two patches for the sash
phone or laptop to record, on a tripod or something that will not wobble
your Sprout's things, counted out and waiting where they will sit

steps.title: Ten minutes, four acts, and the cold open
steps.body:
This is the longest speech of your life so far, and you have already stood inside every part of it. Act one at the first oasis, acts two and three at the second, act four drafted in week 10, the whole thing rehearsed to camera in week 11. Today is not composing. Today is the performance of something you already own.

The cold open first, because it comes before you say a single word.

The Talk opens with a voice, and it is not today's voice. What that voice is was settled before today, privately, by you. Both versions of the opening are real openings, and neither one of them is a consolation prize.

If the old recording exists and you decided you wanted it in the room, play about twenty seconds of it cold. No introduction, no warning, no apology over the top of it. A room that has only ever met you now hears the younger one first, and then you walk out and answer them.

If it does not exist, or if you heard it privately and decided you would rather not put it in front of guests, the act opens the other way and it opens just as well. Read out one thing you actually wrote at the start of the arc, from the journal or the log, in the flattest voice you can manage, and answer that instead. A sentence you wrote years ago, read out cold, does exactly the same job: it puts the distance in the room before you claim any of it.

Either way the rule is the same. Do not explain the opening. Play it or read it, stop, then begin.

Then four acts, one per season, ten minutes for all of them. One prop in your hand per act, held rather than described. Each act says what changed in that season, not what happened in it.

The through-line is yours and it always was. Nobody in this house wrote the sentence you land on at the end, nobody gets to correct it, and if what you decided the four seasons were about surprises the room, that is not a problem with the talk.

One craft note, the one you have been living inside for three seasons and now get to use. Whatever you planted in act one gets paid off in act four. If the room feels the ending coming without knowing why, the plant worked.

And the landing, which is written and does not change: the Talk ends with the Autumn Protocol held up. That page is the last thing the room sees, because what this whole arc was for is what happens after everybody goes home.

steps.title: For the room only
steps.body:
Everybody, this step is for you. Hand the device back after reading it, and read it before they start.

Nobody examines them today. Not with a question, not with a quiz, not with a friendly little test of whether they really know it. They have spent four seasons being asked to prove things and today is not one of those days. They are the host.

During the Talk: no interruptions, no prompting, no mouthing the next line, and nothing helpful whispered from the side. If they lose their place, let the silence sit. They will find it, and a room that waits for a speaker teaches something a room that rescues one cannot.

About the opening. They have chosen how it starts and they settled it privately, before today. Do not ask which version they picked, do not ask why, and if their Sprout is in the room when that voice from a year ago plays, watch the younger one rather than the screen. If either child wants it stopped, it stops immediately and nobody makes anything of it.

Then they judge you. You will debate a motion they wrote, and they will decide who won and read the reasons out loud. Debate properly, take the motion seriously, and then take the decision without arguing with it. If you disagree with the ballot, you may ask them what would have changed their mind, and that is the only question available.

And the last part, which is the actual point of the day. They are going to hand you a page they wrote about the months after this one, and your job is printed on it in their handwriting: belay, never manage. A belayer holds the rope, watches, and does not climb the route for the climber. You will want to improve the page. Do not. Sign it as it stands, and if something on it is genuinely wrong, that is a conversation for a different week.

steps.title: The Expedition Talk
steps.body:
Ten minutes, four acts, one take, camera rolling from before the cold open.

Set the four props in a row where you can reach them without looking, in season order, and pick each one up as its act starts. Held, not described. The room looks at the object while it listens to you.

The cold open runs first and you say nothing over it.

Then act one, the forest. Act two, the coast. Act three, the mountains. Act four, the desert, which is the hard one, because you are still standing inside that season and you have to talk about it as though you can already see it from outside. Two and a half minutes each, roughly, and if one act runs long the fix is to cut a line rather than to speed up.

Act four ends on the landing: the Autumn Protocol, held up, and the sentence you decided this arc was about.

One thing about running long, because you will. A talk that overruns is not a disaster, it is a talk with a line in it that you have not cut yet. If you are over at the halfway mark, cut something on the way rather than racing. Then afterwards, write down what you cut on the day and why, because that is the part of speaking that only ever gets learned in front of people.
checklist: The cold open ran with no introduction and I said nothing over the top of it
All four acts, one per season, with the right prop in my hand for each
Each act said what changed in that season, not just what happened in it
The thing I planted in act one got paid off in act four
The last sentence was mine, and it says what I think the four seasons were about

steps.title: The motion, the debate and the decision
steps.body:
The envelope gets opened in front of everybody. You wrote the motions in week 9 and sealed them in week 11, and you pick one out now, in the room, so that nobody including you can pretend it was chosen to suit the day.

Then you set the round up. Who is on which side is your call, and giving somebody the side they privately disagree with is allowed and is usually the better round. Say the format out loud before anybody stands: how long each speech is, what order, and that nothing new is allowed in a closing.

Then you judge, alone, on your own sheet, and you say nothing at all while anybody is speaking. You have been doing this since week 1 and today it is real: two people you live with, a motion you wrote, and one person deciding.

When it is over, take a real minute in the quiet. Not for politeness, because a decision made in the four seconds after the last speech is usually a decision about who spoke last.

Then read it out loud, standing up, in three sentences. Name the clash, which is the one place the two sides actually met. Weigh it, which means saying why that clash matters more than the others. Then say who won and why, without softening it for the person who lost, and without adding anything to make it land more kindly. The kindness is in the reasons being real.

Then one line each, offered rather than demanded: here is the one thing you could have done that would have changed my mind.
checklist: The envelope was opened in front of everybody and the motion came out of it
I set the format out loud before anybody stood up
I flowed the whole round on my own sheet and said nothing during a speech
The decision named the clash, weighed it and said who won, read out standing up
I told each side the one thing that would have changed my mind

steps.title: The handover, and closing the Atlas
steps.body:
This is the part the whole arc was building towards, and it happens at the table with everybody sitting down.

Read the Autumn Protocol out yourself, off your own page, in your own handwriting. Not a printed version, not one a grown-up typed up neatly. The handwriting is half of what makes it yours.

It says what your weeks look like when nobody is running a season for you. It says the twenty minutes a week that go to a base camp check-in, so that somebody knows where you are without anybody managing you. It says the restart trigger, in your words: two missed weeks in a row is a family conversation and never a punishment. It has the hours spent on paper before the week spends them for you, which is the season 3 idea coming back with your fall as the wallet. And it has the two far dates on it, the ones that have been on the wall map all season, each with a real name beside it, agreed out loud in this room today rather than assumed by anybody.

At the bottom it says what the grown-ups' job is, in three words: belay, never manage. Read that line out loud, then hand them the pen, and let them sign underneath it as belayers.

Then the season book. Say the thing about it you have not said before, and ask the room one question you actually want an answer to.

Then close the Atlas. The coverage ledger is signed, the Protocol goes in, the capsule goes in with its dates in ink on the front, and you say out loud where the Atlas is going to live so that the envelopes can be found by whoever needs them on the mornings they are addressed to.

Then the two patches on the sash, the fourth terrain and the arc, sewn or pinned on by whoever you want to do it.
checklist: The Protocol is one page in my own handwriting and I read it out myself
The page says the grown-ups' job in those words: belay, never manage
Every date on the page has a real name beside it, agreed out loud in the room
The book got its discussion and I asked a question I actually wanted answered
The Atlas is closed with the ledger, the Protocol and the capsule inside, and both patches are on the sash

steps.title: Teach someone younger: their showcase, produced and run by you
steps.body:
Their third showcase, and it belongs to them. You are the producer, which means everything except being the star.

Before they come in: their spot on the floor where everyone can see them, their things counted out and waiting, the family sitting in a row as a real audience with nobody wandering off to fetch a drink. A young child can feel a room that is half paying attention.

Then, before anybody is looking at them, say the thing you agreed in week 11 out loud to them one more time. They can stop whenever they want, the signal is the one you two picked, and nothing bad happens if they use it. A young child who knows they can leave is much less likely to want to.

Then introduce them by name, say what they are going to do in one sentence, and get out of the way.

Four acts, theirs, in whatever order they want them.

The counting. They fill a ten and say ten, then count the extras on top, then do the second ten and say twenty as two whole tens. They count at their own speed and a wobble is part of the act.

The joining story. Some toys, then some more toys, and they say how many now and how they know.

The taking-away story. Some toys go away and they say how many are left and how they know. Ask how they know, once, and then wait however long the waiting takes.

The pattern station, which is the one they have been waiting for. They invent a rule, the whole audience has to copy it, and then they catch whoever gets it wrong. They are the rule maker and nobody argues with the maker. If they want to break their own rule on purpose to catch everybody, let them, because that is the best trick they own.

When they wobble, wait. Do not finish their sentence, do not count for them, do not say the number. You have spent a season learning that one thing per window is the whole of coaching, and today the window is zero things.

Then their page goes into the Atlas beside yours, and you close their showcase the way they like it: sit down with them in front of everybody and read them a book out loud, all the way to the end.
checklist: I set the room before they came in: their spot, their things ready, the family sitting as an audience
I introduced them by name and then got out of the way
They counted to twenty as two whole tens, at their own speed, and they ran their own pattern station
When they wobbled I waited instead of finishing it for them
Their page went into the Atlas and I closed their showcase by reading them a book out loud

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt:
Record the whole Talk in one take, from before the cold open to the last sentence, with the camera framed so your hands and the props are in shot.

Then record two more things. The decision read out after the debate, standing up. And your Sprout's showcase, but only if they said yes to being recorded when you asked them in week 11, filmed by you or by somebody you asked, because it is theirs and they should have it. If they said no, that answer still stands today and nobody reopens it.

Then, alone, with nobody else in the room and the camera still rolling: what did you say today that you could not have said in week 1?
